en: The Ritual for Bestowing the Bodhisattva Precepts,
composed by the Tiantai śramaṇa Zhànrán.

Based on the texts of the ancient masters, as well as the *Brahmajāla*, the *Ratnakaranda-śrāvakācāra*, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, and the works of Gaochang, this ritual prescribes the practice of bestowing the bodhisattva precepts.
The ritual for this matter consists briefly of twelve sections; although it does not rely exclusively on a single school, it does not contradict the sacred teachings.
First, the Opening and Guidance; Second, the Three Refuges; Third, Requesting the Preceptor; Fourth, Confession;
Fifth, Generating the Bodhicitta; Sixth, Inquiry into Obstacles.
Seventh, the conferral of the precepts; eighth, the witnessing; ninth, the manifestation of signs;
tenth, the explanation of signs; eleventh, the extensive vows; twelfth, the exhortation to uphold them.
First, the instructor should initially ask: "What precepts do you wish to receive? The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma is deep and vast."
The ultimate limit is that only through faith can one enter [the path]; because of the presence of faith, the three trainings can be accomplished and awakening can be attained.
Therefore, among the three trainings, precepts are primary. Precepts are the provisions for the broad road to awakening; precepts are the raft for the great ocean of birth and death;
precepts are the excellent medicine for the grave illnesses of the three miserable realms. There are many kinds of precepts: the five, eight, ten, full [monastic], and bodhisattva precepts.

The observance of the five precepts brings retribution as a human or one of the eighty heavens; the observance of the great precepts for renunciation brings the realization of the small liberation, the three insights, and the six supernormal powers, leading to eternal quiescence without remainder.

The Bodhisattva code of discipline, with its eighty thousand subtle practices, brings the fruit of Buddhahood—the three bodies, the four virtues, the marks and signs of excellence, and all uncommon merits.
Now, since you do not seek the minor fruits of humans or devas, but desire only to focus...
To seek unsurpassed bodhi, one must possess six dharmas to obtain the precepts. First, the one capable of bestowing them:

the one who bestows the precepts must first know the categories of beings and the number of people involved; among these, how many belong to the central lands, the borderlands, other paths, or mixed classes?
Though they may have obtained human form, there is no peace or joy, as they are beset by the eight sufferings and tormented by the four snakes. Fourth...
This great danger is fragile and unstable, moment by moment, as the six thieves vie to drive one about through incessant arising and ceasing.

Even if one receives the retribution of other precepts and attains the status of humans or devas, one cannot avoid sinking into the lower realms; nor can one escape the limited fruits of the Two Vehicles and their permanent dwelling in *nirvāṇa*.

Therefore, one must reverently vow to seek the ultimate fruit. Second, regarding the place of reliance: one must first consult and inform [the preceptor], ensuring there are no internal or external obstacles, before establishing the ritual mandala.
First, adorning and purifying the ground so that it is spread out for the recipients to sit upon with stability; second, occupying a high seat to uphold the Dharma;

third, single-mindedly seeking the Great Way; fourth, giving rise to a rare and precious mind—like a pauper, one starving, one who is ill, or one who is terrified, finding treasure, food, a physician, or peace—and not allowing even a single thought of distraction to arise; fifth, if there is no such earnest sincerity, it is all in vain.
Sixth, regarding the mutual exertion of labor: it consists exclusively in seeking the precepts for the benefit of others.

Taking the Bodhisattva’s aspiration to benefit sentient beings as the foundation, one generates great courage and valor, not sparing even body or life, and vows to enter together with all sentient beings into the great ocean of the *tathatā* dharma-realm.

Regarding the second [part], the Three Refuges, one should instruct and say: "Disciple [Name], from this body until the end of the future, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Honored One among Two-legged Beings;
I take refuge in the Dharma, the Honored One who is Free from Desire; I take refuge in the Saṃgha, the Honored One among the Assembly. (Recite three times.

"Disciple [Name] and others, from this body until the end of the future, having completed taking refuge in the Buddha, having completed taking refuge in the Dharma, having completed taking refuge in the Saṃgha..."

The Saṃgha has concluded (recited three times). From this day forward, I take refuge in the Buddha as my teacher and shall no longer take refuge in other demons, heterodox teachers, or external paths.

I pray that the Three Jewels will compassionately accept me; out of their loving-kindness and pity, [may they do so]. (One should explain in detail that the Three Jewels in their Essential Unity are the object of reliance, and further understand that these objects possess distinct characteristics and functions such as sustaining the Dharma.)
Third, regarding the request for the teacher: I have only instructed you to state this yourself, fearing that you might not understand; therefore, I shall now teach you.
"I, [Name], and others, now seek to receive the Bodhisattva precepts from the Venerable One. May the Venerable One, out of compassion and without regard for personal hardship, grant them to us.

This is the request for the teacher who transmits the instruction. Next, one requests the assembly of noble ones to serve as the precept-granting teachers, beginning with the request for the Upādhyāya.
The liturgical text says: "We disciples (so-and-so), etc., respectfully invite Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, to be our Upādhyāya.
Relying upon the Upādhyāya, we shall receive the Bodhisattva precepts. Out of compassion, [we] prostrate once.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva is the Karmācārya; Maitreya Bodhisattva is the Śāstṛ-ācārya; and all Tathāgatas are..."
The Honored One, the Teacher, and all Bodhisattvas are my fellow students and companions (the wording is identical to that for the Upādhyāya).
One should know that the Noble Teacher’s supernormal powers and the eye of wisdom see and hear everything as if it were before one's eyes;

therefore, once the practitioner has requested and obtained a teacher, although they may be facing an ordinary teacher, they should always regard them as beholding a Sage. According to the Gaochang edition, from this point onward there is no longer a section on repentance.

Furthermore, when requesting the precepts, one should first instruct [the candidate] to request them from the Precept Master (Karmācārya), saying: "Virtuous One of noble lineage, now is the proper time; I pray that you will bestow upon me the Bodhisattva precepts.
Next, the Precept Master should rise and make the formal announcement (*jñapti*) to the Honored Teacher (*ācārya*), reciting it three times alone:

"I respectfully announce to all Buddhas throughout the entirety of the empty realm of the ten directions... [The candidate] should then prostrate at the lower end of the platform and rise, reciting alone: "I respectfully announce to all Buddhas throughout the entirety of the empty realm of the ten directions..."

These great Bodhisattvas, [so-and-so] and the others, seek me out and address the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, desiring to petition the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas for the reception of the Bodhisattva precepts.
These [individuals], so-and-so and the others, have already made the great vow and possess deep faith; they are able to relinquish all things and do not begrudge their own bodies or lives.
May the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, out of compassion, bestow upon these [individuals], so-and-so and the others, the purity of the Bodhisattva [precepts].
The Precepts (recited three times).
Fourth, regarding repentance: since beginningless time, who has been without transgression? Or perhaps there are grave offenses that obstruct the arising of the precepts;
it was only after three years that Dharmakṣema finally attained them. Therefore, those of superior faculties and superior practice should [apply themselves accordingly].

In a secluded place, one should separately establish a *maṇḍala*; when practice accords with both principle and phenomenon, performed with sincerity and earnestness, the marks of the highest grade will appear and the category of precepts will spontaneously be perfected.

Now, because those of sharp faculties achieve realization through mere words and conceptualization—due to the addition of present cultivation upon past seeds—and because the formal procedures for the aforementioned matters have already been established, I shall here briefly set forth the ritual for saving the world, generating goodness, and benefiting sentient beings, within which:

Regarding the three [sections], first the intention for repentance is clarified, second the application of the mind is clarified, and third the actual confession of offenses is explained as the method of repentance. First, concerning the "intention":
that which is called the precepts (*śīla*) refers to the dharma of purity; only when the vessel of the dharma is pure is one capable of receiving them.
It is like clean white cloth that easily takes dye. Therefore, one is first taught to repent in order to wash and cleanse oneself, just as one first washes old clothes before [dyeing them].

After using alkaline ash, one must subsequently use pure water; likewise, since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, nearly two thousand years have passed, and the True Dharma has sunk while heterodox winds compete to fan the flames.

Sentient beings, possessing meager merit, are born at this time; even if they hear the teachings, they may occasionally give rise to faith and acceptance, yet it is like drawing on water—it cannot remain for long.
It is difficult to achieve the construction of anything in the air, precisely because the obstacles of delusion are so deep.
If one maintains a profound and resolute adherence, as steadfast as metal struck by a hammer, such that it does not waver from a heart of deep reverence, then transgressions have no way to persist;

yet if transgressions are not extinguished, it is difficult to expect the fulfillment of the categories of precepts. Therefore, one must not hastily receive them. Furthermore, there are three kinds of methods for repentance:
the superior grade of repentance involves casting the entire body to the ground like a great mountain collapsing, with blood flowing from the pores; the middle grade of repentance...
As for those who repent of their offenses in the lower grade, they openly reveal what they have transgressed and weep with tears streaming down as they follow the words spoken by the teacher.
Although this is the lower grade of repentance, they still request all Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas to act as witnesses.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess great compassion and constantly desire to cause all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm to be no different from themselves; although they observe...
Sentient beings are like infants; thus, the practitioner must personally arouse sincere devotion, just as one would invite a Great King.
First, one must purify the dwelling, just as the sun’s orb does not appear in turbid water. All Buddhas of the three periods of time have attained Bodhi by means of this precept (and so forth).
Next, regarding the cultivation of the mind: although one receives the names and categories of the transgressions from the precept master, one must first cultivate [the mind].

Because the ten minds of reversal and conformity extinguish even grave offenses, the Great Master Tiantai established this method in full within the "Text on the Purification of Repentance" in the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation), thereby accomplishing the four samādhis.
Although he has explained it in detail there, I shall now briefly list the names to serve as a wholesome condition for practitioners to extinguish their offenses.
First, regarding the "flowing with the current," this refers to following along with birth and death from time immemorial.

Eleventh, from the subtle to the manifest, they do not transcend these [ten]: (1) recklessly imagining a self and persons; (2) befriending external evil associates; (3) failing to rejoice in the goodness of others;
(4) indulging the three types of action; (5) the pervasive presence of an evil mind; (6) continuity throughout the entire night; (7) concealing verbal transgressions;
(8) having no fear of the evil realms; (9) being without shame or remorse; and (10) repudiating cause and effect. (One must also...)

The teaching relies on names to direct the mind so as to cause transgressions to be extinguished. Next, the "flowing against the current" (*pratiloma*) is explained. As for what is meant by "against the current," it refers to reversing the flow of birth and death by ascending in the inverse order of the preceding "flowing with the current" (*anuloma*).
This is like when one wishes to defeat an enemy, one must first know the enemy's source, origin, and lair;

thus, one knows that it is necessary to proceed from the end toward the beginning. It is like a person who has fallen to the ground rising back up from that very ground. First is right faith in cause and effect; second...

1. Self-reproach and self-rebuke; 2. Fear of the three miserable realms; 3. Confessing one’s flaws and blemishes; 4. Severing the continuity of [unwholesome] thoughts; 5. Generating the bodhicitta; 6.
Cultivating merit to compensate for transgressions; 7. Guarding the True Dharma; 8. Mindfulness of the Buddhas of the ten directions; 9. Contemplating the emptiness of the nature of offenses.

(One must explain and counteract each of these individually; therefore, one knows that obstacles from beginningless time cannot be removed by mere force. Just as one must strike the root when felling a tree or hit the acupuncture point when treating an ailment, one must contemplate these offenses through both the reverse and the direct order.)
Since the nature of these offenses is empty, they are thereby forever extinguished. Having cultivated these ten minds, one speaks as follows:

"I reverently address the Triple Gem throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space in the ten directions—Śākyamuni, the future Maitreya, the twelve divisions of the sutras, the ocean of the treasury of True Suchness, and all the great Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas—to bear witness as we lay bare our confession and repentance from time immemorial."

From the time they first arrived until this very day, throughout that entire interval, they have all been deluded by the false conception of a self and others, and by the immeasurable afflictions of greed, hatred, and ignorance, which have disturbed their bodies and minds.
They have given free rein to the three karmas, fully committing the ten evils, the five heinous crimes, and the four grave offenses;

they have become icchantikas who deny cause and effect (a detailed enumeration of the characteristics of the ten evils, the five heinous crimes, the four grave offenses, and the denial of cause and effect follows), and they have destroyed monasteries and set them ablaze.
Violating the four modes of conduct of the Sūtra-piṭaka; causing the death of sentient beings; stealing the property of the Triple Gem or the wealth of other realms;

engaging in perverted sexual misconduct that defiles the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*); violating one’s father, mother, a *bhikṣu*, a *bhikṣuṇī*, a male human, a female human, or any male or female among animals, ghosts, or spirits;
deceiving the Triple Gem; slandering the teachings of the Three Vehicles; and claiming that [the Buddha] is not the Buddha.
To speak of obstacles and hindrances; or to drink alcohol and eat meat with a lack of compassion; or to consume the five pungent roots (*pañca-garaka*) and thereby defile the Three Jewels;
or to strike, revile, or scold any renunciant—whether they possess the precepts or not, whether they uphold them or break them;
or to cause harm to any sentient or non-sentient being—such transgressions as these [are not...].

One may enumerate and know [the transgressions] committed by oneself, those for which one instructed others, and those witnessed or rejoiced in; before the Three Jewels, one discloses and repents them all.
Aligning with what the Buddhas know, one dares not conceal anything. After this single confession, one shall forever sever the continuity [of these acts] and dare not commit them again.
One vows that the offenses be extinguished. May the Three Jewels, out of their compassion, bear witness. Having recited this three times, one says: "I wish to enter the ocean of the Buddhas."
Faith is the basis for birth into the family of the Buddha; because precepts are the foundation, there are the three refuges up to the bodhisattva precepts.

Those who receive the five, eight, or ten precepts are like walking at night by candlelight: what they see is not far-reaching. Those who receive the precepts of the Hīnayāna are like wandering under the moonlight;
although it is not yet the great brightness of day, it is still superior to a candle. If one receives the Mahāyāna precepts, it is as if being in the sun.
Within it, there is nothing not clearly understood; it can destroy the eight difficulties and enable one to escape the eight sufferings.
It brings one far from birth and death, fulfills the two adornments, perfects the four virtues, and subdues the four māras (and so forth).
Regarding the fifth arousal of the bodhicitta: one should first maintain mindfulness of the Buddhas of the ten directions as the fruit to be attained.

Therefore, the Sūtra says: "If one is able to mindfully recollect the Buddha, one shall perceive the Buddha-mind. Furthermore, the Buddha-mind takes compassion (*karuṇā*) as its foundation, and compassion is preceded by the great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*).
Thus, the great vows serve as the cause for Bodhi. (Having explained this in full, he causes them to arouse the four great vows. He then arouses the great vows.
Furthermore, one adds four further states of mind and accomplishes the Four Great Vows: first, to regard all sentient beings as no different from the Buddha;
second, like a king; third, like one's parents; fourth, like one's elders. Why is this? Because the Buddha is the Dharma King, who is the object of one's seeking;
because there is no distinction between the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings; and because a king is honored within his kingdom, while parents are revered within the home.
The Honored One, as the most venerable among the lower classes, conceives the notion of the fruit within the causes of birth; were it otherwise, how could he deliver humanity?
To deliver sentient beings, he established the remaining three vows. Furthermore, he gave rise to four kinds of resolve:
first, to share all merits performed with others; second, to vow that all sentient beings transcend the afflictions of birth and death.
The Great Ocean has three vows: first, to attain thorough understanding of the definitive meaning of all sutras together with sentient beings;

second, to reach Bodhi together with sentient beings. These are also alternative names for the Four Great Vows; since benefiting living beings is their foundation, one directs one's thoughts toward sentient beings in both cases.
Since the Four Great Vows take benefiting living beings as their basis, once the mind has been resolved, the three karmas become pure.
It is like a bright mirror, clear and transparent both inside and out, capable of receiving the pure precepts;
for by means of this category of precepts, one fulfills the three clusters (*triskandha*), as these three clusters universally encompass all phenomena.

Regarding the sixth question on prohibitions: since one has already been able to resolve the mind, the characteristics of practice are established; these characteristics do not go beyond self-cultivation and the transformation of others.
Because he seeks his own benefit above and transforms others such as yourselves below, you should now understand the characteristics of generating the bodhicitta;

being thus capable of accomplishment, you shall fulfill the Four Great Vows. This is merely the present mental and physical inclination toward practice. If there are obstacles or hindrances, the precepts will not be generated.
As the Brahmajāla Sūtra says: "If one has the seven obstructions, one should not receive [the precepts]. I now ask you: should I...?
If you answer truthfully or do not answer truthfully, you will merely bring suffering upon yourself and others and achieve nothing;
to falsely claim the title of Bodhisattva is to deceive all sentient beings, to betray the Buddha’s heart, and to unworthily receive offerings. Have you never shed the blood of a Buddha?
[You should answer: "No. Have you never killed your father? No. Have you never killed your mother? No. Have you never killed your preceptor (upādhyāya)? No. Have you never killed...? No.

The Ācārya must not be one who has broken the *karmavācanā*, nor one who has split the Saṃgha, nor one who has killed a noble person (*ārya*). If one is free from the seven obstacles (*saptāvaraṇa*), one is capable of receiving the precepts.

You should now arouse a mind of focused concentration and a mind of earnest devotion. As you are about to receive the precepts, you must give rise to the mental state that produces the category of the precepts.
If you can apply yourself with single-minded resolve, like an upright vessel, you will achieve success; even a single moment of deviation will cause failure.
It is like an overturned vessel that can never hold anything;

yet this precept, though it has no form or color, can flow into your body and mind until the end of the future, enabling you to achieve great fruition. Even then, you will have no conscious awareness of it.
Furthermore, when it enters your body, it makes a sound like the crumbling of heavens and the splitting of the earth; therefore, you must maintain constant mindfulness.
One must not entertain other thoughts or other mental deliberations (it should be explained in full that taking an object as the condition is the causal basis for the arising of the precepts).
Regarding the seventh [step], the formal conferral of the precepts: first, the three characteristics are briefly indicated, followed by the formal conferral of the precepts.

As for the three characteristics, they are the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint), the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering virtuous dharmas), and the *sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla* (precept of benefiting sentient beings); one must extensively distinguish these three aggregates (*tri-skandha*).

The characteristics of being extensive, skillful, impartial, and perfect constitute the basis for the practitioner’s aspiration. If it were otherwise, the formal reception of the Dharma would not be accomplished;
for even in the Hīnayāna, there are names for the three aggregates (*triskandhaka*). Next, as for the one who formally receives the Dharma, they should speak these words:
"Listen attentively! You now seek to receive all the pure bodhisattva precepts from me; you seek to receive them all..."

The bodhisattva training precepts—namely, the morality of restraining oneself, the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas, and the morality of benefiting sentient beings—these pure moralities and these training precepts have been received, studied, understood, practiced, and perfected by all bodhisattvas of the past;
they shall be received, studied, practiced, and perfected by all bodhisattvas of the future; and they are being received, studied, practiced, and perfected by those of the present.
"All you Bodhisattvas who are now receiving, now learning, now understanding, and now practicing [this path], and who shall become Buddhas in the future:
from this body until the end of the future, throughout that interval, you must not commit any transgressions. Can you uphold this? (Three questions and three answers.
At the time of the first round, one should say: "Upon all objects throughout the ten directions and the Dharma-realm, the subtle and wondrous precepts are entirely..."
It will not remain long in motion; it should enter into your body. For the second time, one should immediately say:

"This wondrous precept-dharma arises from all phenomena within the Dharma-realm and gathers throughout the void of space, converging upon the crown of your head—subtle, exquisite, and lovely, like a cloud-palace of radiance.
For the third time, at the beginning, one should again indicate, saying: "If [it remains] for one more time..."
The wondrous Dharma of the precepts shall enter your body, pure and perfect; it is precisely at this moment that you receive the precepts.

You must not harbor other perceptions or thoughts so as to ensure the precepts remain without leakage. Having completed the third recitation, he says: "One who possesses such speech is indeed a Bodhisattva and a true son of the Buddha.
Thus, the Mahāyāna Sūtra states: "The initial resolve and the ultimate goal are not two different things; these two minds are one, with the former mind being the latter."
Question:
Regarding the eighth proof, the Preceptor of the Precepts (*śīlācārya*) should perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*) for the recipient as follows:

"The sole disciple (so-and-so) respectfully addresses all Buddhas throughout the ten directions and the entirety of the realm of empty space; in this world-system, within one four-continent world (*cāturdvīpaka*), in the south..."

In the land of the Great Tang, the sovereign of Jambudvīpa, within the monastery at [Name of District] and [Name of County], before the Buddha image, many disciples have come to me to request and receive the Bodhisattva precepts. Having completed this, I have acted as their witness.
I pray that all Buddhas likewise act as witnesses (recite three times). I entreat all Bodhisattvas also as previously stated (recite three times).
Ninth, regarding the manifestation of signs: since the recipients possess three grades of mental states, the manifested signs also differ according to these three grades.
These are various distinct signs such as cool breezes, extraordinary fragrances, sounds, and lights.
When these signs appear within the ten dharma realms, those bodhisattvas each ask their respective Buddha: "For what causes and conditions has this sign appeared? To which that Buddha [replies].

He replied to those bodhisattvas, saying: "This sign has appeared [in such-and-such a direction, such-and-such a realm, such-and-such a country, and such-and-such a place] because many sons of the Buddha, having requested and received the bodhisattva precepts three times from their teacher, have now invited us to serve as witnesses.
Because I am acting as a witness, this sign has appeared. Those bodhisattvas each rejoiced and said to one another regarding these matters: "In such cases as these..."
That beings in such extremely evil states, possessed of such fierce afflictions and evil karma, can give rise to such supremely excellent resolve is truly rare;
therefore, one should feel deep compassion and develop a firm mind for the holy life (*brahmacarya*) toward you all.
Since even the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions give rise to this resolve, you should likewise maintain it with a sincere heart.

One who guards the prohibitive precepts without sparing even body or life, ensuring they are not violated, possesses the marks of the superior grade; the superior wind, superior fragrance, and superior radiance, etc., follow this same principle for the middle and lower grades.
Only a Buddha can fully comprehend these; others have no such ability to know them.

The tenth [section], the explanation of the characteristics, refers to a brief presentation of the observance and violation [of the precepts]. Just as for the Śrāvakas there is a brief exposition of the four pārājikas, so too in the Mahāyāna there is a brief presentation of ten types.
Since it is easier to maintain what is easy to hold and more difficult to recognize what is hard to know, these ten should be explained first. The collective name for these ten is *pārājika*;

this is a term from the Sanskrit language (*brahman*), which in this land [of China] has been translated as "defeat" (*tā-sòng-chù*). It is so called because it defeats one's wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*) and their benefits.

That which is already termed one's own unwholesome dharmas (*akuśala-dharma*) that harm oneself is designated as "self"; if unwholesome dharmas increase and damage wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*), it is called the "place of overcoming others" (*parābhava-sthāna*).
However, regarding the maintenance and violation [of precepts], even down to a single needle or a single blade of grass throughout one's life, all are termed maintenance and violation.
Now, we speak according to what is easily recognized and where the obstruction and damage are profound (and so forth).

(First) If a bodhisattva has already completed the threefold request for the reception of the bodhisattva precepts from a preceptor, yet subsequently kills another, or instructs others to kill, or constructs pits and traps, or provides medicinal substances or contrivances to humans or non-humans—such a person is not a true bodhisattva but a bodhisattva in name only;
being shameless and devoid of remorse, they have committed a pārājika offense. From this body forth...
"Until the end of the future, throughout that interval, will you be able to refrain from transgressing and maintain this [precept]? (He answers: "I am able to maintain it.
(2) Whether one steals by oneself, or instructs another to steal, or steals five *kārsāpaṇas* or more than five *kārsāpaṇas*;

(3) whether one burns, buries, or destroys the color of these five great elements or five sensory objects; or commits sexual misconduct with humans—male or female, gods, ghosts, spirits, or male animals.

Fourth: To engage in impure conduct with a woman; Fifth: To falsely claim that what is not real and not one's own attainment—such as having attained dhyāna, liberation, meditative concentration, the nine successive dhyānas, or the first stage of faith up to the stages of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi) and Sublime Enlightenment (vibuddha)—or to claim that devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits have come to make offerings to me, and so forth;
Sixth: To sell various types of liquor, and so forth; Seventh: To speak of bodhisattvas, whether ordained or lay, as having committed transgressions.

(7) To commit any one of the ten *pārājika* offenses; (8) to falsely praise oneself for actual attainments while disparaging bodhisattvas, whether monastic or lay, by claiming they have committed one of the ten grave offenses or any one of the forty-eight minor offenses;
or to be stingy with the Dharma or stingy with material wealth, refusing to explain even a single word or phrase of the Dharma to those who come seeking it.
Verse 9: Not giving away even a single needle or blade of grass from one's wealth, but instead responding with verbal abuse and insults. Verse 10:
If one feels anger toward any monastic or lay bodhisattva, or toward non-bodhisattvas, devas, ghosts, or animals, one must offer repentance and apology. Verse 11:

If one slanders the Triple Gem by exaggerating, diminishing, contradicting, or engaging in frivolous conceptualization regarding it—even down to a single phrase—whether at the beginning or the end [of the teaching], this constitutes a transgression from the initial precepts through to the conclusion; such acts are likewise considered untruthful and identical [to the aforementioned faults].
First phrase).

Regarding the eleventh, the "Extensive Vows": although the preceding sections on receiving the precepts constitute the ritual for a bodhisattva who has merely initiated their practice, since benefiting others is the fundamental essence, it is necessary to further augment this with vows. The teacher should instruct as follows: "Disciple [Name], etc., I vow that..."
I dedicate the merit arising from this repentance, receiving the precepts, and generating the bodhicitta to all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm.
I vow that those sentient beings in the Dharma-realm who have not yet escaped suffering may be freed from it; those who have not yet attained happiness may attain it;
those who have not yet generated the bodhicitta may generate it; and those who have not yet severed evil and cultivated goodness may sever evil and cultivate goodness.
May those who have cultivated goodness but have not yet gathered the Buddha-dharma gather the Buddha-dharma; may those who delight in benefiting sentient beings quickly benefit them;

and may those who have not yet attained Buddhahood swiftly attain it. Furthermore, by this merit, may all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, upon casting off this body, be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss before Amitābha Buddha, where they shall hear the True Dharma and realize the patience of non-arising.
Possessing great supernormal powers, they travel throughout the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas, constantly hearing the unsurpassed True Dharma of the Mahāyāna.

Through the accumulation of merit and wisdom, they transform themselves and others, being born before the presence of Buddhas in the ten directions so that all Buddha-dharmas may swiftly reach full perfection.
Furthermore, by virtue of these merits, they vow that from this day forward, together with all sentient beings, they shall not fail to attain [liberation] within the gate of their own practice.

May I, prior to attaining the patience of birth (*utpatti-kṣānti*), forever leave behind the bodies of the three evil realms, forever leave behind low-born bodies, forever leave behind female bodies, and forever leave behind bodies subject to bondage.
May I always, within the Buddha-dharma, purely cultivate all practices;

through the gateway of benefiting others, may I manifest divided bodies throughout the lands of the ten directions, constantly acting as a great spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) for sentient beings, showing them the right path and causing them to produce the fruit of reality. May it be so!
Sentient beings who hear my name shall resolve their minds on Bodhi; those who see my body shall sever evil and cultivate goodness;
those who listen to my teaching shall attain great wisdom; and those who understand my mind shall immediately achieve Perfect Enlightenment. Having made this vow, they pay homage to the Triple Gem.

The twelfth instruction: Once those who uphold the precepts have received them, they must understand the prohibitions and the methods of restoration, just as one who has taken excellent medicine must know its dietary restrictions and restorative regimens.
To personally sever evil is the prohibition; to cultivate goodness for the benefit of others is the restoration.

Therefore, one must fully possess these two modes of upholding and universally practice all virtues while universally abandoning all evils, diligently practicing compassionate salvation with reverence.
Regarding the Three Jewels (and so forth), one must in every single practice provide protection through vows, constantly contemplating the fulfillment of the Four Great Vows.
Without for a single moment departing from the Six Perfections and the Four Immeasurables, one employs the gate of wondrous observation to harmonize the myriad realms.

With both principle and phenomena fully realized, one cultivates the primary and auxiliary practices in union, whereby the ten stages of the Perfect and Sudden vehicle transcend the ten objects of contemplation.
The Ritual for Bestowing the Bodhisattva Precepts (Concluded)
